questions.knowledge_point: Simplifying an Expression by Factoring Alternative Forms of the Secant-Tangent Identity
questions.worked_solution:
First, we recall the different forms of the secant-tangent Identity:

$$
\begin{aligned} & (1) & 1+{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x \\  & (2) & {tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x-1 \\  & (3) & {sec}^{2}⁡x-{tan}^{2}⁡x=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can rewrite our expression using $(2),$ as follows:

$$
\frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡x-1}{{tan}^{2}⁡x}=\frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡x-1}{{sec}^{2}⁡x-1}
$$

Finally, we can further simplify our expression by factoring the denominator as a difference of squares, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡x-1}{{sec}^{2}⁡x-1} & =\frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡x-1}{(\operatorname{sec}⁡x+1)(\operatorname{sec}⁡x-1)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{(\operatorname{sec}⁡x-1)}}{(\operatorname{sec}⁡x+1)\cancel{(\operatorname{sec}⁡x-1)}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sec}⁡x+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡x-1}{{tan}^{2}⁡x}=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sec}⁡x+1}.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we recall the different forms of the secant-tangent Identity:

$$
\begin{aligned} & (1) & 1+{tan}^{2}⁡\theta ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & (2) & {tan}^{2}⁡\theta ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta -1 \\  & (3) & {sec}^{2}⁡\theta -{tan}^{2}⁡\theta =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can rewrite our expression using $(2),$ as follows:

$$
\frac{{tan}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta +1}=\frac{{sec}^{2}⁡\theta -1}{\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta +1}
$$

Finally, we can further simplify our expression by factoring the numerator as a difference of squares, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{sec}^{2}⁡\theta -1}{\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta +1} & =\frac{(\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta -1)(\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta +1)}{\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta +1} \\  & =\frac{(\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta -1)\cancel{(\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta +1)}}{\cancel{(\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta +1)}} \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta -1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\frac{{tan}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta +1}=\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta -1.
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to $({tan}^{2}⁡x+1)^{2}-2{sec}^{2}⁡x+1?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we recall the different forms of the secant-tangent Identity:

$$
\begin{aligned} & (1) & 1+{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x \\  & (2) & {tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x-1 \\  & (3) & {sec}^{2}⁡x-{tan}^{2}⁡x=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can rewrite our expression using $(1),$ as follows:

$$
({tan}^{2}⁡x+1)^{2}-2{sec}^{2}⁡x+1=({sec}^{2}⁡x)^{2}-2{sec}^{2}⁡x+1
$$

Finally, we can use simplify our expression and use $(2),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}({sec}^{2}⁡x)^{2}-2\cdot {sec}^{2}⁡x\cdot 1+{1}^{2} & =({sec}^{2}⁡x-1)^{2} \\  & =({tan}^{2}⁡x)^{2} \\  & ={tan}^{4}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
({tan}^{2}⁡x+1)^{2}-2{sec}^{2}⁡x+1={tan}^{4}⁡x.
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${tan}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we recall the different forms of the secant-tangent Identity:

$$
\begin{aligned} & (1) & 1+{tan}^{2}⁡\theta ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & (2) & {tan}^{2}⁡\theta ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta -1 \\  & (3) & {sec}^{2}⁡\theta -{tan}^{2}⁡\theta =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can rewrite our expression using $(1),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{tan}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,({tan}^{2}⁡\theta +1) \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{sec}^{2}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can further simplify and use $(2),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {sec}^{2}⁡\theta  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta } \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta } \\  & ={tan}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sec}⁡\theta  \\  & =({sec}^{2}⁡\theta -1)\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{tan}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =({sec}^{2}⁡\theta -1)\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta .
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to $({sec}^{2}⁡x-1)^{2}+2{tan}^{2}⁡x+1?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we recall the different forms of the secant-tangent Identity:

$$
\begin{aligned} & (1) & 1+{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x \\  & (2) & {tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x-1 \\  & (3) & {sec}^{2}⁡x-{tan}^{2}⁡x=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can rewrite our expression using $(2),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}({sec}^{2}⁡x-1)^{2}+2{tan}^{2}⁡x+1 & =({tan}^{2}⁡x)^{2}+2\cdot {tan}^{2}⁡x\cdot 1+{1}^{2} \\  & =({tan}^{2}⁡x+1)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can use $(1),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}({tan}^{2}⁡x+1)^{2} & =({sec}^{2}⁡x)^{2} \\  & ={sec}^{4}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
({sec}^{2}⁡x-1)^{2}+2{tan}^{2}⁡x+1={sec}^{4}⁡x.
$$
